title: The Invariant Subset R^G: Fixed Points of a Group Action
content: `InvariantSubset G R` is the set of elements r ∈ R such that g • r = r for all g ∈ G. This is the ring-theoretic formalization of 'G-fixed points', the central object of invariant theory. The definition uses Lean 4's `Set R` type with predicate `{r : R | ∀ g : G, g • r = r}`, requiring `MulAction G R` to be in scope.
mathContext: $R^G = \{r \in R \mid \forall g \in G,\ g \cdot r = r\}$. For a polynomial ring $R = k[x_1,\ldots,x_n]$ with $G$ acting by coordinate transformations, $R^G$ is the ring of polynomials invariant under all group elements. Hilbert's 14th problem asks: when is $R^G$ finitely generated as a $k$-algebra? The answer is 'always' for reductive $G$ (Hilbert-Mumford-Haboush) and 'sometimes' for non-reductive $G$.

title: Reynolds Operator: The Linear Retraction Enabling Finite Generation
content: `ReynoldsOperator G R` is a structure encoding a projection ρ : R → R satisfying: (1) ρ is the identity on R^G; (2) ρ maps into R^G; (3) ρ is additive; (4) ρ commutes with multiplication by invariants: ρ(s·r) = s·ρ(r) for s ∈ R^G. These four axioms are precisely what make the invariant ring R^G a finitely generated R^G-module: for any r ∈ R, `ρ(r)` is in R^G and the module structure is controlled.
mathContext: A Reynolds operator is a splitting of the inclusion $R^G \hookrightarrow R$ as $R^G$-modules. The key algebraic consequence: if $R$ is a finitely generated $R^G$-algebra and $\rho$ is a Reynolds operator, then $R^G$ is Noetherian. Proof: $R^G = \rho(R)$ is a direct summand as $R^G$-module; apply the Noetherian quotient theorem. Reductive groups always admit Reynolds operators (averaging over Haar measure in char 0, Haboush's theorem in general). Non-reductive groups generally do NOT — this is WHY their invariant rings can fail finite generation.

title: Reynolds Operator is Idempotent: ρ ∘ ρ = ρ
content: `reynolds_idempotent` proves ρ.proj (ρ.proj r) = ρ.proj r for any r : R. The proof is `ρ.proj_invariant _ (ρ.proj_mem r)`: since `ρ.proj r` is already in R^G (by `proj_mem`), and `proj_invariant` says ρ is the identity on R^G, applying ρ again gives the same element. This is the hallmark of a projection / retraction: projecting twice is the same as projecting once.
mathContext: $\rho \circ \rho = \rho$ since $\text{Im}(\rho) = R^G = \text{Fix}(\rho)$. Algebraically: ρ is an idempotent in $\text{End}_k(R)$. This means $R$ splits as $R = R^G \oplus \ker(\rho)$ as $k$-vector spaces (though not necessarily as rings). The one-line proof `ρ.proj_invariant _ (ρ.proj_mem r)` elegantly shows that both fields of the structure conspire to give idempotency: `proj_mem` says the output is invariant, and `proj_invariant` says ρ fixes invariants.

title: R^G as a Subring: The Algebraic Structure of Invariants
content: `invariantSubring G R` constructs a `Subring R` with carrier `InvariantSubset G R`. The proof obligations are: `zero_mem'` (smul_zero), `one_mem'` (smul_one), `add_mem'` (rw [smul_add, ha g, hb g]), `mul_mem'` (rw [smul_mul', ha g, hb g]), `neg_mem'` (rw [smul_neg, ha g]). Each uses the distributivity laws from `DistribMulAction G R` and `MulDistribMulAction G R`.
mathContext: The invariant set $R^G$ is a subring: if $g \cdot a = a$ and $g \cdot b = b$, then $g \cdot (a+b) = g\cdot a + g\cdot b = a+b$, $g \cdot (ab) = (g\cdot a)(g\cdot b) = ab$, $g\cdot(-a) = -(g\cdot a) = -a$. This requires the action to be by ring automorphisms, encoded by `DistribMulAction` (distributes over $+$) and `MulDistribMulAction` (distributes over $\cdot$). The `Subring R` type in Mathlib packages these closure properties cleanly.

title: reynoldsSum: The Unnormalized Reynolds Operator for Finite Groups
content: `reynoldsSum r = ∑ g : G, g • r` is the sum of all group translates of r. This is the canonical construction of a Reynolds operator for finite groups: dividing by |G| (when invertible in R) gives a true Reynolds operator. The `noncomputable` qualifier is needed because the sum over `Fintype G` uses classical logic. The key downstream theorems show it maps into invariants, is additive, and equals |G|·r on invariants.
mathContext: $\rho_{\text{sum}}(r) = \sum_{g \in G} g \cdot r$. For char 0 or char not dividing $|G|$: the normalized $\rho(r) = \frac{1}{|G|}\rho_{\text{sum}}(r)$ is a Reynolds operator. The averaging trick: left translation by any fixed $h$ permutes $G$, so $h \cdot \rho_{\text{sum}}(r) = \sum_g (hg) \cdot r = \sum_{g'} g' \cdot r = \rho_{\text{sum}}(r)$. This is the finite group analogue of integration over Haar measure.

title: reynoldsSum Maps into Invariants: The Reindexing Argument
content: `reynoldsSum_mem_invariant r` proves `reynoldsSum r ∈ InvariantSubset G R`. The proof: expand the sum, push the scalar through (`Finset.smul_sum`), use `← mul_smul` to write as `(a·g) • r`, then apply `Equiv.sum_comp (Equiv.mulLeft a) (· • r)` — left multiplication by a is a bijection on G, so summing over G and over aG gives the same result.
mathContext: $a \cdot \rho_{\text{sum}}(r) = \sum_g a \cdot (g \cdot r) = \sum_g (ag) \cdot r = \sum_{g'} g' \cdot r = \rho_{\text{sum}}(r)$ where the third step reindexes $g \mapsto ag$ (a bijection). The Lean proof uses `Equiv.sum_comp` to formalize the bijection argument. This is the standard averaging trick: left translation by a fixed group element permutes the group, so the sum is invariant. `Equiv.mulLeft a : G ≃ G` encodes the bijection $g \mapsto ag$.

title: Reynolds Sum on Invariants: ρ_sum(r) = |G| · r
content: `reynoldsSum_on_invariant r hr` proves that for r ∈ R^G, `reynoldsSum r = Fintype.card G • r`. Proof: since `g • r = r` for all g (by `hr`), the sum `∑_g g • r = ∑_g r = |G| • r`. The `simp_rw [hr']` rewrites each `g • r` with `r`, then `Finset.sum_const` and `Finset.card_univ` compute the constant sum.
mathContext: $\rho_{\text{sum}}(r) = |G| \cdot r$ for $r \in R^G$. This shows the normalized $\rho = \frac{1}{|G|}\rho_{\text{sum}}$ satisfies $\rho(r) = r$ for $r \in R^G$ — i.e., it is the identity on invariants, confirming it is a Reynolds operator. The condition 'char not dividing $|G|$' ensures $|G|^{-1}$ exists in $R$. The Lean proof uses `nsmul` ($\mathbb{N}$-scalar multiplication) since $|G|$ is a natural number, and `Finset.sum_const` converts a constant sum to scalar multiplication.

title: GrosshansSubgroup: The Key Concept for Non-Reductive Invariant Theory
content: `GrosshansSubgroup G H` is a typeclass with field `quotient_fg : True` — a placeholder for the true statement that k[G/H] is finitely generated, which requires AlgebraicGroup infrastructure not yet in Mathlib. Despite being a stub, the `class` declaration makes the concept a first-class Lean object: theorems can be stated as 'assuming [GrosshansSubgroup G H], then...' and Lean will track the dependency.
mathContext: $H \leq G$ is a Grosshans subgroup iff $k[G]^H$ (invariants under right $H$-action) is finitely generated as a $k$-algebra, equivalently iff $k[G/H]$ is finitely generated. Grosshans (1997): this condition is equivalent to $k[V]^H$ being finitely generated for ALL $G$-representations $V$ (when $G$ is reductive). The criterion reduces an infinite family of questions (one per representation) to a single question about $G/H$. Known Grosshans subgroups: finite groups, tori, unipotent radicals of parabolics (Seshadri), observable subgroups.

title: Finite Groups Are Always Grosshans Subgroups
content: `finite_group_grosshans G H [Fintype H]` proves `GrosshansSubgroup G H` trivially (since the class field is `True`). The mathematical content: for finite H, k[G/H] ≅ k[G]^H has a basis indexed by the (finitely many) cosets, so it is finitely generated. In characteristic not dividing |H|, the averaging operator (1/|H|)·Σ_{h∈H} h also gives a Reynolds operator directly (the `reynoldsSum` construction from this file).
mathContext: Finite $H \leq G$ $\Rightarrow$ Grosshans: $k[G/H]$ is finitely generated because there are finitely many cosets. More concretely: $R^H$ is a module over $R^G$, and by the Reynolds sum, $R^H$ is a finitely generated $R^G$-module whenever $R$ is (Hilbert's theorem applied to the finite orbit). This is the simplest non-trivial case of Grosshans's theorem. For $H$ finite, invariant theory is always well-behaved: $R^H$ is fg if $R$ is fg as a $k$-algebra.
